body:
Why electricity storage is useful

Solar and wind electricity may be abundant at a time when consumers do not need all of it. Later, electricity demand may increase or renewable output may decrease. Energy storage helps manage this difference between the time electricity is available and the time it is required.

Storage absorbs energy during a charging period and releases part of that energy during a discharge period. It therefore provides flexibility by shifting usable energy from one time to another.

Storage does not create additional net energy. Energy is lost during charging, storage and discharge. The electricity recovered is generally less than the electricity originally used to charge the storage system.

Battery Energy Storage Systems

A Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) stores energy through electrochemical processes. Electricity is supplied to the battery while charging. During discharge, the stored chemical energy is converted into electrical energy that can be supplied to suitable loads or to the grid.

A battery connected to a solar installation can charge when solar production exceeds immediate needs. The stored energy can later help supply electricity after sunset or during a temporary reduction in solar output, subject to the battery's available charge and operating limits.

Battery systems can also respond to short-term changes in electricity demand or generation. Their usefulness depends on how much power they can deliver and how much energy they have stored.

Pumped Storage Hydropower

Pumped storage hydropower stores energy by moving water between reservoirs at different elevations. It is a form of energy storage, although electricity is produced when the stored water is released through a turbine.

Charging or pumping phase

When suitable electricity is available, pumps move water from a lower reservoir to an upper reservoir. The elevated water stores gravitational potential energy.

Discharging or generation phase

When electricity is required, water is released from the upper reservoir through a turbine to the lower reservoir. The turbine drives a generator, converting part of the stored potential energy back into electrical energy.

Pumped storage requires appropriate reservoir arrangements and suitable geographical or constructed elevation differences. It should be distinguished from ordinary hydropower generation, in which water from a natural river or reservoir is used to generate electricity without necessarily being pumped uphill for storage beforehand.

Battery and pumped storage compared

FeatureBattery storagePumped storage
Stored form of energyElectrochemical energyGravitational potential energy of elevated water
Charging processElectrical energy charges the battery.Electrical energy pumps water uphill.
Discharging processBattery releases electrical energy.Water drives a turbine and generator.
Typical grid useEnergy shifting and responsive grid supportEnergy shifting and flexible hydropower generation

Neither technology can deliver unlimited electricity. The available stored energy determines how long a particular discharge can continue. Power capability determines the rate at which electricity can be delivered. Both quantities matter when assessing a storage system's possible contribution.

What is renewable-energy curtailment?

Renewable-energy curtailment is the deliberate reduction of electricity generation below the amount that could otherwise be produced from the available renewable resource under the prevailing conditions.

For example, a wind farm may have enough wind to produce electricity but be instructed to reduce its output because the connected network cannot safely accommodate the full generation. Similarly, solar output may be reduced when available generation exceeds what the system can use or transfer while maintaining secure operation.

Curtailment may occur because of insufficient demand at a particular time, transmission congestion or other system-security requirements. It is not the same as low generation caused directly by weak sunlight or low wind speed.

Ways to reduce avoidable curtailment

Where technically and operationally feasible, several measures can help the grid use more available renewable electricity:

  • Storage: Charge batteries or pump water using electricity that would otherwise be difficult to use immediately.
  • Demand response: Move suitable consumption into periods of abundant renewable generation.
  • Transmission: Transfer electricity to connected regions where it can be used.
  • Flexible generation: Reduce output from suitable other generating sources when renewable generation increases.
  • Forecasting: Anticipate likely renewable output and arrange balancing resources in advance.

These measures can reduce unnecessary curtailment, but they do not guarantee that curtailment will disappear. Some curtailment may remain necessary when electricity cannot be accommodated safely or when suitable balancing options are unavailable.

An example of daily balancing

Consider a sunny afternoon when solar output is high and local electricity demand is moderate. The grid may use available solar electricity to serve current consumers, charge storage and supply suitable flexible demand. If additional electricity can be transferred to another region, transmission may provide another use for the surplus.

Later, as sunlight decreases, stored energy can be discharged, flexible generating stations can increase output and participating consumers can reduce or postpone some electricity use. These are complementary methods for meeting changing grid conditions.

Prelims focus

  • Battery storage converts electrical energy into stored electrochemical energy and later releases electricity.
  • Pumped storage uses electricity to raise water and generates electricity when water flows downward through a turbine.
  • Energy storage shifts electricity use across time; it does not create net energy.
  • Curtailment is deliberate reduction of otherwise available renewable generation.
  • Transmission, storage, demand response and flexibility can reduce avoidable curtailment.
  • Trap: A fall in solar output because of clouds is not, by itself, curtailment.

[Sources: United States Department of Energy, 'Solar Integration: Solar Energy and Storage Basics', sections on energy storage and pumped-storage hydropower; United States Department of Energy, 'Pumped Storage Hydropower', section 'What is Pumped Storage Hydropower?'; International Energy Agency, Renewables 2025, chapter 'Renewable electricity', discussion of curtailment and system integration; International Energy Agency, Renewables Integration in India, 2021, executive-summary sections on storage and flexibility; consulted 16 November 2026.]

body:
Why Gujarat is important for renewable integration

Gujarat has favourable conditions for both solar and wind energy development. Its western and northwestern regions, including Kachchh, offer important renewable-energy opportunities. Parts of coastal Gujarat and Saurashtra also have wind resources suitable for consideration in wind-energy development.

Solar generation depends on sunlight, while wind generation depends on prevailing wind conditions. These resources may be abundant in generating areas that are some distance from cities, industries and other major electricity consumers. Their integration therefore depends not only on the generating plants but also on the electricity network and its ability to manage changing output.

From renewable generation to consumers

Consider a solar or wind installation in Kachchh. The electricity produced at the site must enter a suitable network and reach consumers through available transmission and distribution arrangements. If output rises, the system must accommodate the additional generation. If output later falls, other resources must contribute more or suitable demand must change.

A region with abundant renewable generation may export electricity to other regions when transmission capacity is available. If a network connection is constrained, the electricity may not be transferable even when the renewable resource is strong.

Gujarat's electricity-system institutions

The Gujarat Energy Transmission Corporation Limited (GETCO) performs the role of State Transmission Utility in Gujarat. Transmission infrastructure helps move bulk electricity between generating sources, substations and major demand areas.

The State Load Despatch Centre (SLDC) coordinates electricity scheduling and grid operation within the state. Its functions include monitoring grid conditions and coordinating the operation of generating resources and the transmission system.

The Gujarat Electricity Regulatory Commission (GERC) is the state electricity regulator. It issues regulations affecting electricity-system operation and the integration of renewable resources within its jurisdiction.

Forecasting and regulation in Gujarat

GERC issued the Forecasting, Scheduling, Deviation Settlement and Related Matters of Solar and Wind Generation Sources Regulations, 2019. These regulations addressed forecasting and scheduling of solar and wind generation connected to the state system, helping connect expected renewable production with grid-operation requirements.

The Gujarat Electricity Grid Code, 2026, notified through Notification 09 of 2026 and published in the Gujarat Government Gazette on 7 October 2026, provides a more recent general framework for intrastate grid operation. It assigns the SLDC responsibilities relating to demand estimation, forecasting of wind and solar generation, identification of generation reserves and assessment of demand-response capacity.

GERC also listed its Grid Interactive Distributed Renewable Energy Sources Regulations, 2026, dated 30 October 2026, as part of the state's regulatory framework for distributed renewable electricity. These dates identify published regulatory instruments available by the content cutoff of 16 November 2026; they are not figures describing the present quantity of renewable generation.

Smart metering in Gujarat

Smart-meter deployment is also relevant to Gujarat because the national Revamped Distribution Sector Scheme supports smart metering of consumers and electricity-distribution infrastructure. These meters can improve the collection of consumption information and help utilities understand patterns of electricity use.

Smart-meter information and renewable-generation forecasts concern different parts of grid operation. Smart meters primarily help measure and communicate electricity use, while renewable forecasts estimate expected electricity production. Both forms of information can support better decisions, but neither directly replaces electricity generation, transmission or storage.

How the main technologies work together

A renewable-rich electricity system may face 2 different kinds of balancing situations. During periods of abundant solar or wind generation, it needs ways to use, store or transfer available electricity. During periods of reduced renewable output or high demand, it needs ways to increase usable supply or reduce flexible consumption.

The major solutions therefore perform different functions:

  • Smart meters provide consumption information and support communication with electricity utilities.
  • Distributed generation produces electricity near consumers, including through rooftop solar installations.
  • Microgrids coordinate local loads and resources and may operate independently when properly equipped.
  • Demand response changes when or how much electricity consumers use.
  • Forecasting estimates future renewable generation and electricity demand.
  • Transmission moves electricity between generating regions and consuming areas.
  • Operating reserves provide available response capability when conditions differ from expectations.
  • Storage shifts usable energy between different time periods.
  • Curtailment reduces otherwise available renewable production when the system cannot accommodate all of it.

Applying the concepts to a Gujarat example

Suppose wind and solar generation are abundant in western Gujarat during a particular afternoon. Forecasts help the system operator anticipate the available electricity. Transmission can carry some generation toward demand centres. Batteries or pumped storage may absorb part of the surplus, while suitably flexible consumers may shift some electricity use into the same period.

If the system cannot safely accommodate the remaining renewable electricity, some generation may have to be curtailed. Later, if wind or solar output decreases while demand remains high, available storage, flexible generation, electricity transfers and demand response can help restore the balance.

The important conclusion is that renewable integration is not simply the installation of more solar panels or wind turbines. It also requires the ability to measure, forecast, transfer, store and balance electricity as supply and demand change.

Prelims focus

  • Kachchh and other suitable parts of Gujarat have important solar and wind resource opportunities.
  • GETCO is Gujarat's State Transmission Utility.
  • The SLDC coordinates scheduling and real-time electricity-system operation within the state.
  • GERC issued solar and wind forecasting and scheduling regulations in 2019.
  • The Gujarat Electricity Grid Code, 2026, was published on 7 October 2026 and addresses renewable forecasting and balancing resources.
  • GERC's Grid Interactive Distributed Renewable Energy Sources Regulations, 2026, are dated 30 October 2026.
  • Trap: A renewable-rich region still needs transmission capability and grid flexibility; high installed renewable capacity alone does not guarantee uninterrupted delivery.

[Sources: NCERT, India: People and Economy, Class 12, chapter 'Mineral and Energy Resources', printed pp. 82–83; National Institute of Wind Energy, India's Wind Potential Atlas at 120m above ground level, summary and Gujarat resource coverage; International Energy Agency, Renewables Integration in India, published 12 July 2021, executive summary and Gujarat State Power System Model discussion; Gujarat Electricity Regulatory Commission, Forecasting, Scheduling, Deviation Settlement and Related Matters of Solar and Wind Generation Sources Regulations, 2019, Gazette publication 19 January 2019, sections 4–5; Gujarat Electricity Regulatory Commission, Gujarat Electricity Grid Code, 2026, Notification 09 of 2026, Gazette publication 7 October 2026, sections 1.1 and 8.2–8.4; Gujarat Electricity Regulatory Commission, RE Regulations directory, entry for Grid Interactive Distributed Renewable Energy Sources Regulations, 2026, dated 30 October 2026; Ministry of Power, Press Information Bureau, 'Progress on Smart Meter Installation under RDSS', 2 February 2026; all online sources consulted 16 November 2026.]
